new_statements.rule_in_words: Mahou is described as a two-tone (H vs L) language with the syllable as TBU and tone melodies specified per morpheme; there is no statement assigning stress to any syllable position. The only 'stress' the source recognises is a lexical, binary, whole-morpheme diacritic ('morpheme stress', marked with the stress sign on the morpheme) that is unpredictable (lexically listed: c. 40% of nouns, 26% of adjectives, <5% of verbs) and whose sole effect is tonal: a stressed word-final morpheme attracts the following floating word-boundary H% or phrase accent H* (upstep) onto itself, an unstressed one lets it float rightwards; the feature is neutralised when the morpheme is not word-final. The author explicitly says this is not word stress (syllable prominence) and that he finds no evidence of metrical foot structure above the morpheme (p. 29). Bamba 2005 (LDC intro, saved) independently calls Mawukakan 'a pure tonal system opposing a high tone to a low tone' with two plain (/H/, /L/) and two 'accented' (/H(L)/, /LH(L)/) lexical patterns specified per morpheme, not per syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; not applicable (no syllable-level stress described).
new_statements.exceptions: Morpheme stress only takes effect when the stressed morpheme is word-final (neutralised word-internally, e.g. noun + adjective); the H* accent surfaces on at most one syllable; monosyllabic H verbs in intonational-phrase-final position behave specially (§6.2.3); some dialectal variation (Koonan, Dioman vs Ouaninou) in which lexemes are stressed.
new_statements.domain_note: The 'stress' feature is a property of morphemes, realised via floating tones at phonological-word and phonological-phrase edges; citation forms of nouns (noun + definite article ò) diagnose it (stressed nouns take L article and host H% themselves: sǒ ò 'the horse' vs unstressed cɛ̀ ô 'the man'). Nothing is said about phonetic syllable prominence, duration or intensity within words.
new_statements.identity_note: Brennsæter 2024 describes Mahou as spoken in Ouaninou (Bafing region, western Côte d'Ivoire) with consultants from Ouaninou, Tutie, Koonan, Dioman and Mandougou; he notes minor tonal dialect differences (e.g. Koonan traits) but treats them as one language = maho1249. Bamba (1991, 2005) and Liberman (1995) call the same language 'Mawu / Mawukakan'; Creissels and Ebermann call it 'maukakan' / 'Mauka'. All = Glottolog maho1249, ISO mxx. Not to be confused with Koro (kfo, Creissels' 'korokan') or Wojenaka (jod).

sources.note: Mahou is a two-level (H/L) tone language, TBU = syllable, tone lexically specified per morpheme (pp.22-23). Posits a lexical binary feature 'morpheme stress' (an abstract metrical strength of whole morphemes, ~40% of nouns, ~26% of adjectives, <5% of verbs) that determines whether a following floating boundary tone H% or phrase accent H* docks onto the morpheme; explicitly 'should not be confused with word stress, which specifies which syllable within a word is more prominent' (p.23 fn.3; p.7). sources.citation: Bamba, Moussa. 2005. Introduction. In: Mawukakan Lexicon (LDC2005L01). Philadelphia: Linguistic Data Consortium.
sources.note: 'Mawukakan is a pure tonal system opposing a high tone to a low tone. Those two basic tonal patterns (/H/ and /L/) combine with two accented patterns /H(L)/ and /LH(L)/ in the lexical items of the language.... the word bears in general one of these four tonal patterns, independently of its length. In other words, tones patterns are specified at the level of the morpheme or lexical unit, not the syllable.' Syllables always open. No word-stress position stated; refers to Bamba 1991 for the tone/accent analysis.

sources.citation: Green, Christopher R. 2018. A survey of word-level replacive tonal patterns in Western Mande. Mandenkan 59: 67-108.
sources.note: Second-hand (from Ebermann 1986: 54-57, Bamba 1984, Creissels 1982): Mahou monomorphemic words have four lexical melodies /H(L)/, /H(H)/, /L(H)/, /L(L)/ (associated tone + post-segmental floating tone); compound tone examples. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Creissels, Denis. 1987. Compte-rendu: Ebermann, Erwin, Die Sprache der Mauka (Dissertationen der Universität Wien 181, 1986). Mandenkan 13: 89-91.
sources.note: Review (scanned). Describes Ebermann's tonology as positing a lexical 'post-segmental' floating tone on every unit; says the Mahou tone system (esp. the 'supra-haut' tone) 'reste encore à élucider'; criticises Bamba's (UQAM) accent-based theorising as over-ambitious. Nothing on word stress; indicates Ebermann's grammar treats prosody purely tonally.
